companies.description: Amazon's bar leans on Leadership Principles and scenario thinking more than raw algorithm difficulty. Coding rounds skew toward OOD and under-specified prompts that reward clarification skill, and a GenAI-usage behavioral question appears in nearly every modern loop. Bar Raiser independence and writing-heavy work samples shape the senior-level signal.

Uber's loop leans heavily on Uber Eats and rider/driver marketplace problems — Cart pricing, geo heatmaps, surge, and restaurant recommendation surface in nearly every onsite at L5+. Coding rounds are mostly tagged LeetCode patterns, but Hack2Hire OAs ship a small rotating set of original problems that rarely appear elsewhere. Coding bar is the gate; system design quality drives leveling between L5a / L5b / Senior / Staff.

Apple interviews are unusually team-owned: the same company can run classic LeetCode screens, MLE case studies, hardware verification drills, project deep-dives, and system design loops with little advance disclosure. The strongest pattern is role fit: interviewers probe whether your prior work maps directly to the team's product surface, data domain, and engineering stack, while still expecting clean code, concise trade-off reasoning, and polished behavioral stories.

Google's loop runs on hiring-committee arbitration, with a separate team-match phase deciding whether HC approval turns into an offer. Coding bars are remarkably consistent across teams; leveling rigor and behavioral depth drive most of the L3–L6 differentiation.

ByteDance / TikTok runs a strict one-round-at-a-time funnel with sharp org-by-org variance in bar, language, and round mix. Coding rounds skew toward classic LeetCode-medium with one self-built test case; MLE and SRE loops front-load 30+ minutes of oral 八股 before any code is written. Interviewer professionalism varies — strong candidates drive the round structurally rather than waiting to be assessed.

Meta sits mid-transition between two interview loops in 2026. The legacy track still drives most candidates through CodeSignal-style OAs and tightly time-boxed coding rounds, while a new AI-Native loop layers in AI-assisted coding, AI-Enabled system design, and an AI-oriented behavioral round on top. Which track you land in depends on org and recruiter, not candidate preference.

OpenAI pairs an unusually high raw-coding bar with explicit no-AI-tools rules during most interviews — a deliberate contrast with the product. Phone screens often run a single multi-part simulation for the full hour, and senior loops add deep ML and research-grounded system-design rounds that probe mechanism, not vocabulary.

Waymo loops mix nominally LeetCode-style coding with deliberately ambiguous, autonomy-flavored prompts and a signature 'data fluency' round that's hard to drill for. Coding bars are mid-hard but interviewers frequently swap in original problems framed around self-driving scenarios; ML and senior loops add a behavior-prediction-style ML system design round on top.

Microsoft runs two parallel hiring tracks: the standardized Hiring Event (HE) loop covering Azure, Cloud, Copilot, and Office orgs, and Mustafa Suleyman's MAI org with its own recruiter pool and a distinctly OpenAI-flavored coding rotation. The HE bar is consistent — four 60-minute rounds back-to-back on a fixed weekday — with medium-difficulty algorithms and one system-design slot; MAI loops add project deep-dive depth and pull problems from an in-memory-DB / beam-search / streaming-decoder pool that does not overlap with classic LeetCode prep.

Stripe favors long realistic prompts in a full IDE — integration, debugging, refactor — over LeetCode-style algorithms. System design is grounded in payments and regulatory reality, and behavioral signals weigh ownership and written communication as heavily as raw technical depth.

Oracle's loops split along two clear axes: OCI (Cloud Infrastructure) runs a fairly standard LC + system-design loop with heavy Indian interviewer rotation, while OHAI (Oracle Health, the post-Cerner business unit) leans into OOD/class-design problems built around healthcare scenarios. Coding bars are mostly easy-to-medium, but interviewer variance and post-loop down-leveling / ghosting are unusually common — the loop result often determines the eventual level, not just the yes/no.

Airbnb's loop is famously consistent and famously slow. The coding pool is small and reused — a candidate who has drilled the canonical questions (split-stay, terrain water-drop, KV store, code review) walks in advantaged. Differentiation happens in the code-review round, the experience deep-dive, and the standalone core-values round, which is calibrated separately from the rest of the loop and serves as a real gate. Expect strong technical performance to land in a multi-week team-match queue rather than a fast offer.

Roblox interviews lean heavily on a small, stable repertoire of coding and system design prompts drawn from the company's own product surface — rate limiting, like-button counters, matchmaking queues, delayed payments. The bar is high but predictable: interviewers want bug-free implementations with crisp boundary handling and design discussions that ground every trade-off in real platform scale (millions of concurrent players, hot creator experiences, cross-region latency). HM and director rounds heavily probe past experience with comparable traffic and scope.

Capital One's engineering loop is unusually predictable: a long CodeSignal OA gates everyone, then a single Power Day stitches four 45-60 minute rounds — coding, system design, case study, and behavioral — back to back. The technical bar is moderate but the case study and BQ rounds carry real weight, especially for MLE / Applied Research / Data Science where the business-context framing of a model decision is the differentiating signal.

Pinterest's loop leans hard on a recurring custom prompt library — escape-room state-tracking, trie-backed access control, ads/log aggregation, splitwise-style settlement — over canonical LeetCode. ML system design is split into two distinct rounds ("ML Practitioner" and "ML System Design") that effectively cover the same recommender / retrieval / ranking surface from two angles, with embedding-heavy product framing throughout. Fully-remote, front-loaded compensation, and long team-match windows define the experience as much as the technical bar.

Goldman Sachs interview loops lean heavily on traditional LeetCode-style coding — the firm publishes its own tagged problem list on LeetCode, and the OA / phone screens recycle from a stable bank that maps closely to it. Behavioral signal is concentrated in a Hirevue video screen with tight 30-second prep windows, and quant-flavored desks (GSAM, Quant Engineering) layer probability and statistics drills on top of the standard coding bar.

LinkedIn's loop pivoted heavily in 2025 — Staff candidates now sit a packed two-round phone screen (coding + project retro) before a five-round onsite that includes an AI-Coding session in CoderPad's assistant pane. Behavioural depth is the dominant downlevel axis; the same coding bar that passes at Senior frequently caps a Staff loop with a downlevel offer.

Citadel and Citadel Securities run two distinct loops sharing one brand. Citsec (the market maker) hires for HFT software, quant research and quant dev; its phone screens lean on small, sharp coding prompts (merge-K, ring buffers, stock-DP ladders) and the loop is famously single-fail — any weak round and the next interview is cancelled within a day. Citadel (the hedge fund) and its sub-orgs (GQS, EQR, NXT) lean harder on probability brainteasers, deep resume drilling and a multi-week team-match stage where coding bar drops but cultural and PM-style fit dominates the offer decision.

Salesforce's loop is bank-driven: a small set of coding prompts (LFU Cache, Flatten JSON, linked-list dedup, frontend curry + traffic light, OA HackerRank classics) and one signature system design (Coffee Ordering, with its SQL follow-ups) cover the bulk of recent rounds. Down-leveling at offer time is common — the HM screen and behavioural depth materially shape the final level, often more than coding correctness alone.

Databricks interviews are unusually bank-driven: candidates who know the recurring prompt families often recognize the round within the first few minutes. The loop mixes algorithmic coding with low-level systems and product-grounded design, then puts real weight on behavioral, hiring-committee, and reference signals after the technical rounds.

DoorDash's loop is dominated by a small, slow-moving library of original Code Craft prompts (Dasher Pay, Bootstrap API, Round Robin debugging) plus a handful of recurring system-design favorites (3-day Donation, Notification, Food Review). Coding bar is the gate; system design correctness and behavioral consistency drive leveling. The bar swings sharply with the interviewer — multiple candidates report bug-free coding rounds that still ended in rejection — so prepping the canonical question set cold matters more than chasing breadth.

Anthropic runs an unusually small, transparent technical question bank — the recruiter typically names which prompt family you'll see days before the round, so candidates can target preparation precisely instead of guessing. Bars are calibrated for problem-solving velocity and follow-up depth rather than novelty; offers are decided by hiring committee + reference check, and the culture round on AI-safety alignment is the single most common rejection point even for candidates who clear every technical stage.

Bloomberg's loop is a coding-heavy gauntlet: three back-to-back technical rounds each pack two LeetCode-style problems with little hand-holding, plus an HR screen and an engineering manager round that anchors on a single deep project story. The coding bar emphasizes pristine communication — dry-running, edge cases, and complexity discussion are graded as heavily as the solution itself, and interviewers routinely push for second-best alternatives even after a working answer. New-grad and tech-screen verdicts often arrive within hours, while jump-shift onsites favor candidates who can explain past trade-offs without prompting.

Optiver is a market-making trading firm whose interview process is built to find fast, calibrated decision-makers under pressure. The funnel is dominated by a heavy online assessment — a probability/sequence/reaction battery for quant roles and OOP simulation coding for engineers — and the quant loop centers on a live EV betting game where speed and bet-sizing matter more than ending profit.

Coinbase runs a long, gated pipeline — AI recruiter screen, a cognitive aptitude test, a culture/personality questionnaire, and a CodeSignal coding OA all precede the recruiter call, and team match still happens before the 4-round VO. Coding rounds bias toward multi-level CodeSignal-style problems (banking system, in-memory database, mining-block knapsack, crypto order management) over canonical LeetCode; bring your own scaffolding because interviewers often hand you a blank file with no class structure or tests. AI-assisted coding is now an explicit round on its own.

Akuna Capital interviews lean heavily into the firm’s trading DNA: fast arithmetic, probability, market-making intuition, and implementation details that resemble exchange or trading-engine code. Quant roles can move through multiple asynchronous assessments before a superday, while developer tracks mix HackerRank-style coding, C++ debugging, data-structure design, and practical rate-limit or order-book exercises.

JPMorgan Chase's engineering loop is predictable but operationally uneven: a light HackerRank-style OA is followed by a Super Day with coding, code review, system design, and behavioral rounds rotating across candidates. The technical bar skews practical: simple algorithms, review of production-ish Java code, concurrency/style critiques, and system designs around traffic, search, inventory, payments, and URL routing.

xAI's loop is built around speed and founder-style intensity: a single 15-minute video screen often gates the entire pipeline, the take-home assumes you will use Cursor / Claude Code, and onsite rounds run in person in Palo Alto with offers decided minutes after the final round. Bars are calibrated less for algorithmic novelty than for raw shipping velocity, low-level systems instincts (concurrency, GPU/inference, distributed numerics), and willingness to work 60–100 hour weeks RTO5.

Snap interviews are highly interviewer-dependent: candidates report classic graph and cache problems, open-ended backend coding, product-heavy system design, and MLE loops that dig into recommendation systems, ranking, fundamentals, and project judgment. The safest preparation strategy is to be fluent in BFS/DFS, cache/data-structure implementation, feed and ads design, and concise behavioral stories around innovation, ambiguity, and execution.

Walmart's engineering loop runs through Karat / HackerRank phone screens followed by a three-to-four round virtual or in-person onsite covering coding, system design, behavioral, and an extended Team Fit phase. Coding bars are moderate but heavily weighted toward Java / Spring Boot fluency, and the system-design slot leans toward retail and logistics prompts (membership, delivery, ticketing, sensor ingestion). The Team Fit phase that follows technical approval is unusually long and team-shopping in nature, and is responsible for a meaningful share of loop attrition.

Tesla interviews are highly team-specific: Autopilot, Optimus, Dojo, data engineering, infotainment, and factory-software teams each run their own practical technical screens. The common pattern is a fast transition from resume/project discussion into runnable code, with interviewers pushing for optimality, clean implementation style, and concrete ownership of past technical decisions.

SoFi's engineering interviews mix Karat-style screens, practical frontend builds, backend coding, and manager-led project depth. The loop rewards candidates who can clarify ambiguous product requirements, keep implementation details tidy under HackerRank or Karat constraints, and explain trade-offs without drifting away from the requested scope.

NVIDIA interviews are highly team-specific and much less LeetCode-bank-driven than most large tech loops. System Software, Linux, Tegra, DGX AI infra, and Deep Learning roles lean toward engineering scenarios: C/C++ debugging, graph validation, GPU / inference fundamentals, small utility coding, and project deep dives; some design and product-facing AI roles add system-design or technical-marketing discussions.

Atlassian interviews emphasize pragmatic product engineering: API design, backend data structures, careful clarification, and values-driven collaboration. Senior loops add management-signal and leveling weight, while MLE loops still include substantial backend coding alongside recommendation, RAG, and ML systems design.

IBM's recent technical screens are dominated by auto-triggered HackerRank online assessments for entry-level, intern, full-stack, backend, AI, and .NET roles. The question mix is mostly easy-to-medium data structures, sliding-window, interval, graph-connectivity, and small frontend/CSS tasks, while Red Hat / AI-infrastructure loops add live coding around inference kernels, Kubernetes controllers, and DevOps fundamentals.

Figma builds its interviews around its own product surface and runs them as collaborative, test-case-driven pair-programming sessions where candidates pick their own language and prompts are deliberately long and under-specified. Coding signal rewards clean handling of messy object models over algorithmic trickiness; system-design rounds reward pragmatic, right-sized solutions over over-engineering. Since the IPO the bar has tightened, and final leveling is often settled in a separate executive conversation.

Rippling's engineering loop is unusually concentrated: a small set of OOD coding prompts, two data-heavy system-design prompts, and a practical web API round account for most SWE interviews. The bar is driven by speed through multi-part prompts, clean extensible design, and whether the candidate can collaborate with AI tools without losing ownership of the solution.

Cisco's recent technical loops are split between automated OA batches for SWE / intern roles and Meraki-style phone or manager loops. The OA bank leans practical and implementation-heavy: strings, arrays, linked lists, grids, and small dynamic-programming tasks with strict output formatting.

Perplexity interviews lean toward long, product-flavored engineering simulations rather than generic LeetCode. Candidates should expect Python-first coding, incremental multi-part specs, careful edge-case preservation across parts, and system-design conversations tied closely to search, discovery, retrieval, inference, and operational reliability.

Two Sigma's loops split sharply by track: QR and data roles emphasize linear models, statistics, data-analysis case work, and domain reasoning, while SWE/QSE loops favor implementation-heavy trading, database, data-structure, and OOD prompts. The process is fast, high-variance, and often unforgiving on incomplete code or unclear statistical reasoning.

Ramp front-loads a CodeSignal "industry coding framework" online assessment — a four-level progressive object-modeling problem — often before any resume review, then runs a small, heavily-repeated set of live coding rounds. Prompts are deliberately under-specified: printing and exploring the data format yourself is the real signal, and the bar rewards fast, debuggable, pragmatic code over elegance. The loop also explicitly probes how you collaborate with AI tools.

Instacart's recent SWE loop is dominated by CodeSignal-style practical coding: in-memory databases, worker/task trackers, expression parsing, file I/O, and product/inventory consistency. Senior loops now commonly split the onsite into two phases: two coding rounds plus a Karat AI codebase round first, then system design and project deep-dive if the first phase clears. MLE loops keep the same practical coding bar but add a fundamentals-heavy ML concept screen.

Intuit's recent engineering loop is unusually AI-aware: even standard SWE screens often pair a short practical coding task with a separate conversation about using generative AI safely and effectively. New-grad assessment traffic is dominated by mixed-format OA work across Python, SQL, and Bash, while experienced screens skew toward product-flavored implementation and applied data tasks.

Temu (Pinduoduo's overseas arm) runs a fast, recruiter-driven loop conducted largely in Chinese, where every technical round front-loads 20-40 minutes of detailed project deep dive and leaves only 10-20 minutes for an easy-to-medium LeetCode problem. There is no system-design round; for senior candidates the decisive gate is a final director/VP/SVP conversation that scrutinizes project depth and cross-round consistency far more than algorithms.

Shopify's loop is unusually lightweight and behavior-heavy: a cognitive assessment and a long "life story" values interview gate most candidates before any real coding. The signature technical round is a 75-minute AI-assisted pair-programming session where bringing your own AI coding tool (Cursor, Claude Code, Cline, Copilot) is encouraged — the real test is communication, reviewing AI-generated code, edge-case handling, and testing rigor rather than algorithmic difficulty. MLE loops add ML modeling and ML system-design rounds built around Shopify's own product-taxonomy, forecasting, and recommendation problems.

Affirm's loop leans on realistic fintech coding problems—loan aggregation, transaction reconciliation, fraud detection, promotion redemption—run on HackerRank with long boilerplate that rewards careful reading over algorithmic flash. System design centers on experimentation platforms and payment data models; hiring-manager rounds favor 'how did you' probing over scripted STAR. Expect strong signal on requirement comprehension and clean data-structure manipulation, plus a recruiting process that can be slow or go quiet.

Robinhood's loop leans on a small, stable bank of recurring problems: a graph load-factor / referral-count coding question, a Job Scheduler system design, and a stock-quote / trading-system design. Onsites pair these with a project deep dive that is graded as hard as the technical rounds, and interviewers consistently reward complete, edge-case-correct code over elegant-but-unfinished design.

Lyft's engineering loop is hands-on and execution-heavy: candidates repeatedly see practical API-wrapper, in-memory data-store, scheduling, and product-system prompts rather than abstract puzzle rounds. Senior loops add system design around payments, donation flows, web crawling, or marketplace-adjacent products, while frontend and intern tracks lean toward small project-style implementation.

Okta runs a lightweight, team-driven loop with a fast weekly cadence — recruiter call, a short online assessment, one or two interviewer-watched coding rounds, and hiring-manager conversations, with offer decisions made at the team level rather than a central committee. Coding leans practical over heavily algorithmic, and the assessment stack is unusually AI-forward: recent OAs explicitly allow AI tools and lean on hands-on builds against Okta/Auth0's real identity APIs.

MathWorks EDG interviews center on a structured early-career pipeline: HireVue motivation and sponsorship checks, a HackerRank OA with math plus coding or MATLAB, then technical rounds that mix OA review, easy-medium algorithms, OOD, and EDG fit. Preparation should cover non-Python OA languages, MATLAB awareness, project storytelling, and clear understanding of the EDG rotation/support model.

Vanta runs a deliberately small, stable interview loop built around a handful of recycled problems — a topological-sort phone screen, a local-machine `uniq` build, and an internal DAU/MAU analytics design. Difficulty skews easy-to-moderate, but the prompts are verbose and reading-comprehension-heavy, and most rejections trace to requirement-clarification or following the interviewer's instructions rather than raw algorithmic strength.

Scale AI's recent engineering loops are practical and implementation-heavy: candidates are expected to write working code under shared-screen conditions, reason about production readiness, and explain prior ML or product work clearly. MLE loops add NumPy-level model implementation, LLM training theory, and paper or project trade-off discussions, while FDE and enterprise roles lean toward customer-facing AI systems.

Harvey builds domain-specific generative-AI tools for law firms and legal teams, layering retrieval and document-workflow products (Vault / Data Room) on top of frontier LLMs. Its interview loop is small and stable: a single coding screen drawn from a tight rotation, system-design rounds anchored on Harvey's own document products, and a values-driven behavioral bar — with recruiters who actively prep candidates before each round.
